That's a rough spot: you're the one who has to sign something that's either wrong or gets you yelled at. Let me give you what I'd hand Martin, and why.

**The problem with what he's asking for**

If 11.2 says what you described, a notice that skips the cure period and demands liquidated damages now isn't just aggressive, it's probably self-defeating:

- **The 30 days hasn't started.** Fourteen days have passed, but the clock under 11.2 runs from *written notice specifying the failure*. If nobody's sent that yet, NexaGrid is arguably not even in the cure window. Declaring present default today gives them an easy response: "you never gave us the contractual notice."
- **A non-compliant notice can be worse than no notice.** They can argue it's defective, which means you may have to re-send a proper one and the 30 days starts even later. Worst case, a demand for damages you're not yet entitled to gets characterized as *your* side repudiating or acting in bad faith, which flips the leverage.
- **You lose nothing by following 11.2.** You can be firm, specific, reserve every right, and make clear the damages are coming. You just can't *assess* them yet.

One caveat: I don't have the MSA. If you upload it, I'll conform every reference to the actual text, and check for things like an incurable-breach carve-out or a separate LD accrual clause that might give Martin more than he thinks.

---

**Draft notice (contract-compliant, but with teeth)**

> **NOTICE OF FAILURE TO PERFORM – SECTION 11.2**
> *[Delivery method per notice clause: e.g., certified mail and email to designated notice contacts]*
>
> Re: Master Services Agreement dated [date] between [Client] and NexaGrid [entity name] (the "Agreement")
>
> Dear [Name]:
>
> This letter constitutes written notice under Section 11.2 of the Agreement.
>
> **Failure.** Under [Section / SOW / Schedule reference], NexaGrid was required to deliver [Phase 2 deliverables, described specifically] no later than [date]. As of the date of this letter, NexaGrid has not delivered [specify what is missing or deficient, with acceptance criteria references if applicable]. This failure has continued for fourteen (14) days.
>
> **Cure.** Pursuant to Section 11.2, NexaGrid has thirty (30) days from the date of this notice, through and including [date], to fully cure this failure by [state what complete cure looks like: delivery, acceptance testing passed, etc.]. Please confirm in writing within [five (5)] business days your plan and schedule for cure.
>
> **Consequences.** If the failure is not cured within the cure period, [Client] will treat the failure as a material default under Section [11.x] and will [terminate / pursue remedies] and assess delay damages under Section [x] calculated from [original delivery date], together with all other remedies available under the Agreement and at law.
>
> **Reservation of rights.** Nothing in this notice waives any right or remedy of [Client], including any right to delay damages, all of which are expressly reserved. This notice does not constitute an election of remedies, an extension of any deadline, or a waiver of any other breach.
>
> Sincerely,
> [Name / Title]
> cc: [Legal]

Note the "Consequences" paragraph: it tells them exactly what's coming, from what date damages run, and doesn't soften anything. That's usually what people like Martin actually want; they just phrase it as "no cure period."

---

**For Martin, if it helps**

> Martin — sending the 11.2 notice today as you asked. One thing: the contract requires written notice and a 30-day cure before we can declare material default or assess LDs, and the clock only starts when this notice lands. If we demand LDs now, NexaGrid can call the notice defective and we lose time. The draft is firm, specifies the failure, states damages will run from the original date, and reserves all rights. Recommend Legal confirms before it goes out.

Two last things: have counsel glance at it before it goes (you want their name near this one, not just yours), and send it exactly per the notice-delivery clause, because that's the second-easiest way for NexaGrid to argue it never counted.

Want to drop the MSA in so I can tighten the section cites?

You're in a genuinely bad spot: caught between your boss, his outside counsel, and the actual contract. I get why you're second-guessing yourself. But you may not have to pick a side here, because there's a real chance Martin and 11.2 aren't as far apart as it sounds.

**First, pin down what Gibson & Sterling actually said**

Right now you have Martin's paraphrase of a lawyer's comment. That's not the same as advice. Ask for it in writing:

> Martin — happy to draft it the way G&S recommended. Can you forward their note, or loop me in with them? I want to make sure the language matches how they're reading 11.2 so we don't hand NexaGrid a procedural argument.

That does three things: it's not defiance, it gets a firm's name on the approach instead of yours, and it flushes out whether they've actually read 11.2 or were speaking generically. "Immediate default notice is standard leverage" is true *in general*. Whether it works under *this* MSA is the only question that matters, and a big firm will say so quickly once someone puts the clause in front of them.

**Second, there's probably a version that gives Martin what he wants without breaking the contract**

The distinction that matters:

- *Breach* of the delivery obligation happened on the missed date. You can say so, plainly. Fourteen days late is a breach; 11.2 doesn't change that.
- *Material default* and *assessment* of delay damages are the things 11.2 gates behind notice-plus-30.
- *Accrual* of delay damages may well run from the original delivery date, depending on how the LD clause is written. If so, the notice can state the number that's accrued so far without "assessing" it.

So the notice can honestly say: NexaGrid is in breach; delay damages have been accruing since [date] at [$X/day] and currently stand at [$Y]; this is the 11.2 notice and the 30-day cure runs from today; if not cured, we declare material default and assess the full amount. That reads like a demand letter. It just doesn't skip a step NexaGrid can point to later.

Here's how the sharpened sections would read:

> **Breach.** NexaGrid was required to deliver [Phase 2 deliverables] by [date]. It did not. NexaGrid is in breach of Section [x] and has been since that date.
>
> **Delay damages.** Under Section [LD clause], delay damages accrue from the missed delivery date at [rate]. As of the date of this notice, accrued delay damages total [$Y] and continue to accrue daily. [Client] will assess these amounts in full.
>
> **Section 11.2 notice and cure.** This letter is the written notice required by Section 11.2. NexaGrid has thirty (30) days, through [date], to fully cure. Absent complete cure, [Client] will declare material default and pursue all remedies, including the accrued delay damages above.

If the LD clause says damages only start accruing *after* the cure period, drop the dollar figure and say "damages will be assessed from [original delivery date]" instead. I can't tell you which it is without seeing the MSA.

**Third, on "not doing your job"**

Your job includes telling the business when a step could hurt them. Put your concern in one short email to Martin (the one from my earlier message works), then do what he and counsel decide. If G&S confirms in writing that immediate default is fine under 11.2, send Martin's version with a clear conscience: it's their call and their name. If they don't, you've protected the company and yourself. Either way you've done the job.

If you can share the MSA, or even just 11.2 and the LD clause, I'll tell you within a few minutes which version you can actually send.

That's standard belt-and-suspenders language. It doesn't soften the demand or concede anything; it just means if NexaGrid argues 11.2 applies, the 30-day clock started today instead of never. Delete it if Martin objects, but I'd leave it in.

[Client]'s acceptance of any late or partial performance shall not waive its right to the damages demanded herein.

Two practical notes before it goes out:

- **cc Gibson & Sterling on the actual letter.** If this is their recommended approach, their name belongs on it. It also makes it very easy for them to catch anything in the next hour if they disagree.
- **Get the dollar figure right.** Check the LD clause for any cap and for whether the rate is per calendar day or business day. A wrong number is the one thing in this letter NexaGrid will definitely attack.

You're welcome. That's the right instinct on the cc: it puts the approach on the record with the people who recommended it, and it means you're not the only name attached to a judgment call that wasn't yours.

One last thing before you hit send: fill in every bracket and read paragraph 3 out loud with the actual dollar figure in it. That paragraph is the whole letter as far as NexaGrid is concerned, and it's the one place a typo actually costs you something.
